prompt.context: Your client is Contract Manufacturer Co., which produces components for a number of diverse products. They have grown quickly and had 2011 revenues of $17 billion. They now serve 350 customers across nearly 20 industries, including consumer electronics, mobile phones, healthcare, and defense. They are dependent on their end-markets, e.g. how many consumers buy mobile phones next year, but they only "see" this demand through their customers, e.g. Apple and RIM. They are therefore very vulnerable to changes in market demand but find it difficult to estimate this demand. Third party sources, e.g. financial analysts and market research organizations who follow the space, are also very inaccurate. The CEO of Contract Manufacturer Co. has become increasingly frustrated by their vulnerability to the market and their inaccuracy in predicting end-market demand. He wonders whether they should be better able to identify market trends and in particular, whether they could better utilize data they have accessible via their customer relationships.
prompt.question: How would you go about advising the CEO? Should Contract Manufacturer Co. be able to develop a proprietary view of their markets?

clarifying_info.q: What services does Contract Manufacturer Co. provide?
clarifying_info.a: Customers turn to Contract Manufacturer Co. or their competitors to provide parts quickly and cheaply. They are involved in some design and after-market services but most of their business (revenue) comes from simply manufacturing the parts requested. Customers will generally request parts 3 months in advance.
Contract Manufacturer Co. is in a competitive space. They are one of the leading players, with about 10% market share. Their largest competitors are Chinese and Taiwanese.

Contract Manufacturer Co. is structured by industry verticals, which it terms 'sectors,' e.g. mobile phones or healthcare. They have sales and account teams dedicated to customers in these sectors and a VP leads each sector. They have a strategic planning group at the corporate level, but it is quite new and not very mature.
Contract Manufacturer Co. is a profitable business but their margins are only 3-5%, so they depend on volume.
Contract Manufacturer Co. is based in the US but has operations worldwide. Their customers are also global.

clarifying_info.q: What are the main cost drivers?
clarifying_info.a: Costs include procurement of supplies, manufacturing costs, and labor costs. When customers request parts, Contract Manufacturer Co. needs to invest significant sums in machinery and technology.

exhibits.title: Annual revenue forecast errors
exhibits.shows: A bar chart comparing Contract Manufacturer Co.'s forecast error versus third party forecast error for each of 8 sectors and overall. Each sector has two bars side by side. The taller the bar, the greater the forecast error (less accurate).

data.note: Contract Manufacturer Co. is forecasting each sector's revenue for the next year; the third party source is forecasting the size of the overall market (sector) next year

exhibits.title: Sector prioritization matrix
exhibits.shows: A 2x2 matrix with 'Value of a proprietary view' (low to high) on the y-axis and 'Ability to develop a proprietary view' (low to high) on the x-axis. The two dimensions are further described as 'Degree of market exposure / Sector volatility' for value, and 'Ability to develop a proprietary view' for the x-axis. Eight sectors are plotted across the four quadrants.

axes.y_axis: Value of a proprietary view (driven by degree of market exposure and sector volatility)
axes.x_axis: Ability to develop a proprietary view

framework: What: Understand whether other contract manufacturers or proxy industries have developed market intelligence capabilities, and what best practices exist
Why: Clarify the benefits of developing a more accurate view of their end-markets (revenue forecasting, account planning, long-term strategy, investor credibility)
How: Assess customer willingness to share strategy and plans with their supplier
Where: Determine in which sectors the effort is most applicable and highest-impact using a need vs. ability matrix
Who: Identify the right roles and responsibilities within the organization to own market intelligence gathering
When: Outline immediate next steps and a realistic timeline for building this capability

questions.prompt: What do external benchmarks tell us about market intelligence maturity in contract manufacturing?
questions.guidance: In the contract manufacturing space, companies are not mature at market intelligence. Competitors do not appear to be further along. However, best-in-class companies in other industries have established market intelligence functions that capture market data, including publicly available data such as financial statements and research reports. The candidate should acknowledge both the benchmark gap and the opportunity.

questions.prompt: What are the specific benefits of developing a more accurate proprietary view of markets?
questions.guidance: 1. Accurately forecast revenue. 2. Improve account planning, e.g. revise production, capacity, and resource plans. 3. Develop long-term strategy, e.g. identify capability gaps and evaluate need for M&A or R&D to fill those gaps. 4. Build credibility with the investor community by communicating an accurate annual view of the market and corresponding strategy. The candidate should note it is difficult to quantify benefits precisely but the strategic value is clear.

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 1, what are the key insights about forecast accuracy?
questions.guidance: Two key insights: (1) Third party forecasters are just as inaccurate — and in most cases more inaccurate — than Contract Manufacturer Co. at forecasting the market. This means there is a gap that a proprietary approach could fill. (2) Accuracy differs markedly across sectors (e.g., CMC is only 3% off in Sector 1 but 33% off in Sector 6), so the applicability of market intelligence efforts varies by sector. The candidate should begin to think about prioritizing sectors.

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 2, how should Contract Manufacturer Co. prioritize which sectors to focus on first?
questions.guidance: The matrix plots 'value of a proprietary view' (y-axis, driven by sector volatility and market exposure) against 'ability to develop a proprietary view' (x-axis). The top-right quadrant (high value, high ability) represents 'Greatest impact' sectors — many customer relationships, high volatility, less accurate external data — and should be the first priority. The top-left quadrant ('More challenging') has high need but lower ability, requiring more effort. The bottom-right ('Quick wins') has lower volatility but good ability. The bottom-left ('Look externally') has both lower need and lower ability, suggesting reliance on external research instead.

questions.prompt: Would customers be willing to share their strategy and plans with Contract Manufacturer Co.?
questions.guidance: Research indicates most customers were open and willing to discuss their strategies with Contract Manufacturer Co. since they understand it furthers both organizations' objectives. However, customers in certain industries/sectors remain reluctant to share much. The candidate should flag sector-level variation and the need to build trust.

questions.prompt: Who within the organization should own the market intelligence function?
questions.guidance: The centralized strategic planning team could be responsible for gathering and tracking publicly available data. Ultimately the sales and account teams will need to be trained to listen and engage customers in discussions about market direction. There is no single right answer about ownership, but the candidate should address the need for both a central function and distributed execution through customer-facing teams.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the immediate next steps Contract Manufacturer Co. should take to begin building a market intelligence capability?

categories.name: Internal alignment
ideas: Get buy-in for this idea across the organization, including sector VPs and the corporate strategic planning group

categories.name: Sector prioritization
ideas: Perform analysis to understand in which sectors to prioritize efforts, using the value vs. ability matrix

categories.name: Pilot
ideas: Consider running a market intelligence pilot in a few high-priority sectors before full rollout

categories.name: Systems and data
ideas: Evaluate the systems in which they currently capture customer data and ensure they will support more mature data gathering

categories.name: External data
ideas: Begin to more comprehensively track publicly available data such as financial statements and research reports

recommendation: Yes, Contract Manufacturer Co. should pursue a proprietary market intelligence capability. Their competitors are no more advanced, third-party sources are often less accurate than CMC itself, and most customers are willing to share information. The strategic benefits — better forecasting, improved account planning, stronger long-term strategy, and investor credibility — are clear.
The effort should be phased, prioritizing sectors in the top-right quadrant of the matrix (high value, high ability) to generate the greatest impact first, then expanding to other sectors over time.
risks: Building this capability will take time; it will not transform overnight and requires sustained organizational commitment
Customer willingness to share varies by sector; some sectors may have inherent limits on information sharing
The strategic planning function is new and immature, so scaling it will require investment and leadership attention
Thin margins (3-5%) mean limited resources to fund a new intelligence function without clear short-term ROI
next_steps: Secure CEO and VP-level buy-in across sectors
Use the prioritization matrix to select two or three pilot sectors with the greatest impact potential
Launch a market intelligence pilot, testing both customer engagement approaches and public data tracking
Assess and upgrade CRM and data systems to support structured intelligence collection
Define ownership: empower strategic planning to own centralized analysis; train account teams to gather customer intelligence
Develop a timeline and KPIs to measure forecast accuracy improvement over time
